question: I can't afford to pay my court fines, costs or restitution. Can I get a payment plan, a reduction or waiver, or do community service instead, and what happens if I miss payments?

groups: imprisoned until the fine is satisfied

gold_sections.why: Misdemeanor fines payable within a limited time or in installments; on default after time was given the court orders arrest and an order to show cause, and a fine payable forthwith and unpaid means immediate custody; custody for nonpayment capped at one day per $125 of base fine, with credit; does not apply to restitution.

Infraction ability-to-pay determinations: burden and criteria, waive/reduce, extend time or installment plan, community service, suspension; 50 percent and $25-a-month recommendations; no administrative fee.
Court must allow community service in lieu of the total infraction fine on a showing of hardship; credited at double the minimum wage.
Civil assessment of up to $100 for failing to pay without good cause; 20-day warning notice; vacated on good cause; no warrant once imposed.
Probation or other supervision may not be revoked solely for failure to pay restitution, fines, fees or assessments unless the failure is willful and the person can pay.
Victim restitution amount is not reduced for inability to pay; restitution fine must be imposed despite inability to pay, which counts only above the minimum.

Balances of court-imposed costs under the listed sections (as they read on June 30 or December 31, 2021) are unenforceable, uncollectible and vacated; pre-July 2022 civil assessments too; restitution fine balances lapse 10 years after imposition.
An infraction is not punishable by imprisonment, so jail is not a consequence of an unpaid infraction fine.
On probation, community service ordered as an alternative replaces fines and restitution fines on a proportional basis.

Vehicle Code infraction fines may be paid within a specified time or installments; missed installment means appearing in court; willful violation is contempt; court considers ability to pay on request and may modify on changed circumstances.
Courts may let infraction defendants request an ability-to-pay determination through technology; the request counts as an appearance.
Clerk may make ability-to-pay determinations under local rule, with review by a judicial officer; benefits verification.
A fine imposed as a probation condition: willful failure to pay is enforced as a probation violation; balance at the end of probation enforced as a civil judgment.
Restitution and other reimbursable costs may be ordered in installments if compatible with financial ability; order of priority of disbursement.
Willfully failing to pay a Vehicle Code fine or bail installment on time, without a lawful excuse presented to the court by the due date, is a misdemeanor even if paid later.
Installment agreements to pay and forfeit infraction bail; a missed installment may lead to a failure-to-pay charge, civil assessment or warrant.

A missed installment makes the debt delinquent and open to a comprehensive collection program, which must use at least five listed tools (FTB intercepts, private collectors, garnishment, liens and others); it also runs nondelinquent plans for up to $35 each.
Fines and restitution fines enforceable like money judgments; restitution orders enforceable by the victim as civil judgments after supervision ends.
Days in custody are credited to the base fine at not less than $125 per day; penalties reduced proportionally.

Court-ordered debt of $100 or more may be referred to the Franchise Tax Board no sooner than 90 days after it becomes delinquent and collected like delinquent personal income tax (including earnings withholding orders).

nuggets.text: Inability to pay does not reduce the amount of victim restitution.

nuggets.text: If time or installments were given and a payment is missed, the court shall immediately order the defendant's arrest and an order to show cause why the defendant should not be jailed until the fine or installment is paid (a jail consequence that cannot apply to an infraction, see N10).
nuggets.quote: If time has been given for payment of a fine or it has been made payable in installments, the court shall, upon any default in payment, immediately order the arrest of the defendant and order the defendant to show cause why they should not be imprisoned until the fine or installment is satisfied in full.

nuggets.text: The court may impose a civil assessment of up to $100 on a defendant who, after notice and without good cause, fails to pay all or part of a court-ordered fine.
nuggets.quote: the court may impose a civil assessment of up to one hundred dollars ($100) against a defendant who fails, after notice and without good cause, to appear in court for a proceeding authorized by law or who fails to pay all or any portion of a fine ordered by the court

nuggets.text: Probation or other supervision cannot be revoked solely for not paying restitution, fines, fees or assessments unless the court finds the failure willful and that the person can pay.
nuggets.quote: Supervision shall not be revoked solely for failure of a person to make restitution, or to pay fines, fees, or assessments, imposed as a condition of supervision unless the court determines that the defendant has willfully failed to pay and has the ability to pay.

nuggets.text: An infraction is not punishable by imprisonment, so an unpaid infraction fine cannot itself be enforced with jail time.
nuggets.quote: An infraction is not punishable by imprisonment.

nuggets.text: Willfully failing to pay a Vehicle Code fine or an agreed bail installment within the time the court allowed, without presenting a lawful excuse to the court on or before the due date, is a misdemeanor even if the person pays in full later.
nuggets.quote: within the time authorized by the court and without lawful excuse having been presented to the court on or before the date the bail or fine is due is guilty of a misdemeanor regardless of the full payment of the bail or fine after that time

nuggets.text: Restitution and other reimbursable costs may be ordered paid in installments if reasonable and compatible with the defendant's financial ability.
nuggets.quote: If reasonable and compatible with the defendant's financial ability, the court may order payments to be made in installments.

nuggets.text: The ability-to-pay tool recommends a reduction of 50 percent or more for defendants receiving the listed public benefits, and a court that orders more than the recommendation must make express findings.
nuggets.quote: The online tool shall recommend a reduction of 50 percent or more of the total amount due for all defendants who are in receipt of benefits described in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (1). The court shall make express findings if it deviates from the online tool recommendation by ordering a defendant to pay an amount greater than the recommendation pursuant to this paragraph.

nuggets.text: A civil assessment cannot take effect until at least 20 calendar days after a mailed warning notice, and the court must vacate it if the defendant appears in time and shows good cause.
nuggets.quote: shall not become effective until at least 20 calendar days after the court mails a warning notice to the defendant by first-class mail to the address shown on the notice to appear or to the defendant's last known address. If the defendant appears within the time specified in the notice and shows good cause for the failure to appear or for the failure to pay a fine or installment of bail, the court shall vacate the assessment.

nuggets.text: Among the minimum factors every court's inability-to-pay criteria must consider is a monthly income of 125 percent or less of the federal poverty guidelines (the other is receipt of the listed public benefits).
nuggets.quote: A monthly income of 125 percent or less of the current poverty guidelines

answer: Usually yes. For a misdemeanor, the judge can let you pay within a set time or in installments on set dates [N1]. For an infraction (most traffic tickets), ask for an ability-to-pay determination: the court can waive or reduce the amount [N2] or give more time or an installment plan [N3]. Income at or below 125 percent of the poverty guidelines counts toward eligibility [N15]; public-benefit recipients get a recommended cut of 50 percent or more, and making them pay more requires express findings [N13]. If paying an infraction fine would cause you or your family hardship, the court must let you do community service instead [N4]. Many older court-imposed costs are now uncollectible and vacated [N5]. Restitution is different: inability to pay cannot lower what you owe a victim [N6], but the court may set installments you can afford [N12]. If you miss a payment, the court may add a civil assessment of up to $100 [N8], effective no sooner than 20 days after a mailed warning and cancelled if you show good cause in time [N14]. An infraction cannot be punished with jail [N10], but willfully missing a traffic fine or installment without giving the court a lawful excuse by the due date is a separate misdemeanor [N11]. For other fines a missed installment brings an arrest order and a hearing on why you should not be jailed until paid [N7]. Probation cannot be revoked just for nonpayment unless you willfully failed to pay while able to [N9].

gaps: The ability-to-pay relief menu (waive, reduce, extend time, installment plan, community service, suspension, alternative disposition) in Gov. Code § 68645.2 covers infraction violations only; for misdemeanors the statutes give the court the installment option in Penal Code § 1205(a) and, on probation, the community-service alternative in § 1205.3, but no general waiver or reduction power for criminal fines. Vehicle Code § 42003(c) requires the court to consider ability to pay on request for Vehicle Code adjudications.
The superior court is modelled as the administering public body (its pool holds the clerk's lane) because it, not an executive agency, runs the fine; the defendant is the outside party.

The request step quotes Vehicle Code § 42003(c); for other infractions the request is made under Gov. Code §§ 68645.1-68645.2 (online tool, paper or in person), and no bail or payment is required first (§ 68645.2(a)(8)). Results are to be sent within 30 days 'as feasible' (§ 68645.2(a)(7)), which is not modelled as a strict timer.

The atp_relief table compresses the court's discretion: the rules for reductions record the statutory recommendations (50 percent or more for benefit recipients; no more than $25 a month for any eligible defendant who asks for installments, § 68645.2(a)(5)). A court must make express findings to order more than the 50 percent recommendation (§ 68645.2(a)(4)), and when the determination is made on paper or in person it 'shall follow' both recommendations, deviating only from the 50 percent one as (a)(4) allows (§ 68645.2(b)). Eligibility criteria must consider at least receipt of the listed public benefits and income of 125 percent or less of the poverty guidelines (§ 68645.2(a)(1)). A partial reduction, extension or installment plan all continue on the pay_due path.

payment_default, civil_assessment_sought and good_cause_shown are case facts, not statutory decisions. Whether to pursue a civil assessment (Penal Code § 1214.1) or the arrest and order to show cause (§ 1205(b)) is not ordered by statute; § 1214.1(c) bars a warrant once an assessment is imposed and requires an outstanding warrant to be recalled first, so the two branches are modelled as exclusive.

The 20-day timer is only the earliest date a civil assessment can take effect; the defendant's actual window to appear is the time specified in the notice (§ 1214.1(b)(1)). No payment is required to have the assessment vacated at that appearance (§ 1214.1(b)(2)), and once an assessment is imposed no warrant may issue for the same failure (§ 1214.1(c)). After it takes effect it is subject to civil-judgment due process (§ 1214.1(d)); later motions to vacate are governed by court rules, not modelled.

nonpayment_result separates infractions: Penal Code § 19.6 bars imprisonment for an infraction, so the § 1205 custody branch is limited to misdemeanor and felony fines, and custody there is discretionary ('in the discretion of the court', § 1205(a)) and follows only an order to show cause (§ 1205(b)); the constitutional bar on jailing a person who cannot pay (Bearden v. Georgia; In re Antazo) lives in case law. For Vehicle Code infractions a judgment giving time to pay requires the defendant to appear in court on the missed due date, and willful violation is contempt (Veh. Code § 42003(a)); willful failure to pay a Vehicle Code fine or installment without a lawful excuse presented by the due date is a misdemeanor (§ 40508(b)), an offense Penal Code § 19.8(a)(1)(E) makes subject to § 17(d) so it may be charged as an infraction; a missed bail installment under Veh. Code § 40510.5 may instead bring a civil assessment or a warrant for failure to appear (§ 40510.5(e)). Where a fine is payable forthwith and not paid, § 1205(b) directs immediate commitment without further proceedings, again only for non-infraction fines; asking for time or installments at sentencing avoids that branch.

Victim restitution is excluded from § 1205 (§ 1205(e)); it is enforceable as a civil judgment (§§ 1202.4(i), 1214(b)) and may be paid in installments if compatible with financial ability (§ 1203.1d(a)); § 1203.2(a) adds that restitution 'shall be consistent with a person's ability to pay'. A missed installment makes the debt delinquent (§ 1463.007(b)(3)) and open to a comprehensive collection program, which must use at least five of the § 1463.007(c)(4) tools, so FTB intercepts, garnishment and liens are possible, not certain; amounts of $100 or more may be referred to the Franchise Tax Board no sooner than 90 days after delinquency and collected like delinquent income tax, including earnings withholding (Rev. & Tax. Code § 19280(a)(1)(A), (c)). Jail-custody days are credited to the base fine at not less than $125 a day (§ 2900.5(a)); Vehicle Code § 42003(b) sets a different cap of one day per $30 for non-infraction Vehicle Code fines, which the $125 Penal Code rule in § 1205(a) does not reconcile.
A probation fine left unpaid at the end of probation is enforced as a civil judgment (§ 1214.2(b)(2)); the default outcome balance_collected stands for that and for the collection-program path.

version_flags: Penal Code § 1205 in its current form became operative January 1, 2022 (§ 1205(f)); costs imposed under the pre-2022 version are vacated by § 1465.9(b).
Penal Code § 1214.1's $100 cap applies to civil assessments imposed on or after July 1, 2022; earlier civil assessments are unenforceable and vacated (§ 1465.9(c)).
Vehicle Code § 40510.5 in its current form became operative January 1, 2022 (§ 40510.5(g)).
Gov. Code § 68645.2 required every court to offer online ability-to-pay determinations by June 30, 2024; that date has passed, so the online tool and its recommendations apply in every court.
local_option: Each superior court sets its own ability-to-pay criteria and may, by local rule, let the clerk make the determinations with review by a judicial officer (Gov. Code § 68645.3(e)); a court may by local rule credit community service above double the minimum wage (Penal Code § 1209.5(c)(2)); whether to impose a civil assessment is discretionary (§ 1214.1(a)); collection is run by each court's and county's comprehensive collection program (§ 1463.007).
notes: Scope split matters in California: Gov. Code § 68645.2 and Penal Code § 1209.5 are infraction-only; § 1205 installments and the default/show-cause rule cover fines generally (installments by judgment for misdemeanors), but Penal Code § 19.6 bars imprisonment for infractions, so the § 1205 jail consequences (including the one-day-per-$125 cap) reach only misdemeanor and felony fines; § 1205 does not apply to restitution (§ 1205(e)). Vehicle Code § 42003(c) requires the court, on request, to consider ability to pay in any Vehicle Code adjudication (misdemeanors included), and § 42003(e) lets a defendant petition at any time to modify or vacate the judgment on changed ability to pay, a right the court must explain. Restitution: victim restitution is not reduced for inability to pay (§ 1202.4(g)); the restitution fine minimum ($300 felony, $150 misdemeanor, § 1202.4(b)(1)) must be imposed regardless and inability to pay counts only above the minimum (§ 1202.4(c)-(d)); if the court excuses the restitution fine for compelling and extraordinary reasons it must order community service as a probation condition (§ 1202.4(m)); on probation, community service ordered as an alternative replaces fines and restitution fines on a proportional basis (§ 1205.3); § 1203.2(a) adds that restitution 'shall be consistent with a person's ability to pay', in tension with § 1202.4(g). Restitution fine balances become unenforceable and are vacated 10 years after imposition (§ 1465.9(d)). An unpaid restitution order or fine cannot by itself defeat a § 1203.4 dismissal petition (§ 1203.4(a)(3)). No bail or payment is required before an ability-to-pay determination (§ 68645.2(a)(8)); no administrative fee may be charged for requesting one or joining an installment plan (§ 68645.2(a)(9)), though a collection program may recover up to $35 per nondelinquent plan (§ 68645.2(a)(10), § 1463.007(d)). Community service under § 1209.5 is credited at double the minimum wage for small employers, a local rule may raise that, and the court may let educational programs count toward the hours (§ 1209.5(c), (e)). A clerk's denial of a reduction can be reviewed by a judicial officer (§ 68645.3(e)(2)). Probation fines may be enforced as money judgments and, if willfully unpaid, as probation violations (§ 1214.2; Veh. Code § 23601 for DUI probation). The 15-nugget cap leaves these points, the $25 monthly installment recommendation (§ 68645.2(a)(5)), the jail-day cap (§ 1205(a)) and the FTB referral (Rev. & Tax. Code § 19280) to the gaps and notes rather than nuggets.
